items.title: David N. Baker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I’m intrigued by the slaves’ uprisings, Denmark Vesey.

ctx.x: I’m not sure what you say. These are people who were responsible for transforming kinds of experiences. We know their sacrifices. I can remember Dr. King, hearing him the night before, saying, “I may not live to get there.” But that’s an abstract. But I think he saw that as a real possibility, and of course it was a possibility. And the next day he was killed. I think you can’t dwell on those things. I think you have to be constantly aware of the things that shape your destiny, shape your life, and shape the life…

then in America, I read an article this morning in the paper, that people are asking that finally this government apologize to blacks for slavery. People say, “Well, I wasn’t born then. What do I – why me?” But they don’t stop to think of all of the residual effects of slavery. I think as important as the Holocaust in terms of tragedy were the middle passages, where millions of blacks died in the holds of ships, coming to America to be slaves. I can’t dwell on that, but I can comment on it in what I write, in the…
You actually heard Malcolm X speak.
